content:
Oxfam has set up a monitoring station on the rooftop of a building in Yau Ma Tei to collect wet bulb globe temperature data, believing it more accurately reflects the actual heat conditions in the district.

Under the Labour Department's new mechanism for the Work Heat Stress Warning, if the Hong Kong Observatory has already issued an Extreme Heat Warning Special Announcement, a Red Alert can be issued as long as the "Hong Kong Heat Index" reaches 32 at King's Park monitoring station or at two of the remaining nine stations (i.e. "two out of nine"); likewise, a Black Alert at an index of 34 also requires only a "two out of nine" trigger. In addition, when temperatures reach 35°C or above in many parts of the territory, in addition to further lowering the index thresholds for triggering warnings as mentioned above, any existing heat stress warning will automatically be raised by one level.

Dr Leung Ming-fung, Oxfam Hong Kong Programme Director, believes the current approach for issuing "Work Heat Stress Warnings" is inaccurate. Due to the geographical locations of monitoring stations and differences in peak heat periods, he recommends setting up wet bulb globe temperature monitoring instruments in all 18 districts of Hong Kong, and arranging rest breaks for nearby workers according to the situation in each district.

The Observatory's ten monitoring stations that collect heat stress data are located at King's Park, Beas River, Hong Kong Observatory, Sha Tin, Kau Sai Chau, Kowloon Bay, Happy Valley, Wong Chuk Hang, Chek Lap Kok, and Wetland Park. Oxfam has set up its own six monitoring stations in Kwai Chung, Tsuen Wan, Yau Ma Tei, Taikoo, Admiralty, and Tung Chung to collect data.

Dr Leung Ming-fung, Oxfam Hong Kong Programme Director, recommends setting up wet bulb globe temperature monitoring instruments in all 18 districts of Hong Kong, and arranging rest breaks for nearby workers according to the situation in each district.

4.4°C difference in maximum temperature between monitoring stations in the same district

Comparing data from the Observatory and Oxfam, on 9 August, the Observatory's King's Park recorded a maximum 60-minute average wet bulb globe temperature of 32, while Oxfam's monitoring station in Yau Ma Tei recorded 36.6—a difference of 4.4. From 3 August to 8 August, the difference in maximum 60-minute average wet bulb globe temperature between King's Park and Yau Ma Tei ranged from 2 to 3 degrees.

Oxfam provided The Collective with data from its six self-set monitoring stations and used the internationally standard "wet bulb globe temperature" to simulate the "Work Heat Stress Warning" from 3 August to 9 August, finding that over the six days, some districts reached the "Black Work Heat Stress Warning" level and one day saw districts reach the "Red Work Heat Stress Warning" level.

Leung explained that geographical and environmental factors cause a significant temperature difference between the two monitoring stations in the same district. He described the King's Park monitoring station as located in a "paradise," with high altitude and cool air, with no nearby buildings. By contrast, the Yau Ma Tei monitoring station is located on the rooftop of a tenement building in the city, surrounded by many high-rises, which more realistically reflects conditions experienced in buildings or on the streets.

Leung added that most of the Observatory's monitoring stations are set up in open mountainous or rural areas, yet wet bulb globe temperature readings can be significantly affected by the placement of the sensors due to heat stress factors. For example, readings can vary greatly depending on whether the sensor is placed in poorly ventilated locations surrounded by many high-rises. Oxfam's six monitoring stations have their sensors placed near high-rise buildings and refuse collection points to reflect the actual conditions faced by outdoor workers at their workplaces.

Peak heat times differ significantly between monitoring stations

From 15 May 2023 to 15 August 2026, the Labour Department issued a total of 209 "Yellow Work Heat Stress Warnings," but not a single "Red Work Heat Stress Warning" or "Black Work Heat Stress Warning" was issued. Leung explained that the "yellow, red, and black" warnings are so difficult to trigger because the peak temperature periods at different monitoring stations do not coincide, making it difficult in the past to meet the "four out of nine" threshold.

Using the organisation's monitoring station data for 9 August as an example, the peak heat period in Kwai Chung was from 1pm to 2pm; in Tsuen Wan, 3pm to 4pm; in Admiralty, 12pm to 1pm; in Yau Ma Tei, 3pm to 4pm; in Taikoo, 9am to 10am; and in Tung Chung, 11am to 12pm.

Oxfam's monitoring station in Yau Ma Tei is surrounded by many buildings.

At least "6 days of Black" and "1 day of Red" from 3 to 9 August

Oxfam analysed heat stress index data from its six self-set monitoring stations and used the "wet bulb globe temperature" to simulate the "Work Heat Stress Warning" from 3 August to 9 August. The results were: on 9 August and 8 August, six districts reached the "Black" level; on 7 August, five districts reached "Black" and one reached "Red"; on 6 August, four districts reached "Black" and two reached "Red"; on 5 August, four districts reached "Black" and two reached "Red"; on 4 August, two districts reached "Black," three reached "Red," and one reached "Yellow"; on 3 August, two districts reached "Red" and one reached "Yellow."

A worker performs welding on a rooftop during hot weather, surrounded by many buildings under the scorching sun with little ventilation.

Organisation recommends setting up wet bulb globe temperature monitoring instruments in all 18 districts

Leung suggested referencing approaches elsewhere. For example, Singapore requires specific outdoor workplaces, such as large construction sites, shipyards, and processing sites, to install "wet bulb globe temperature instruments," while other locations use data from 13 weather monitoring stations, with each station covering approximately 57 square kilometres on average. By comparison, each monitoring station in Hong Kong covers an average of approximately 558 square kilometres—a tenfold difference.

Cleaning workers on the streets are most affected by weather changes.

Leung believes that wet bulb globe temperature sensors should be installed in all 18 districts of Hong Kong, or even at designated workplaces such as refuse collection points, and that rest arrangements should be made for workers according to the situation of each district or workplace.
